concept: zeroth_law_thermodynamics
is_a: AXIOM
definition: If system A is in thermal equilibrium with B, and B with C, then A and C are in thermal equilibrium. This transitivity defines temperature as a universal, measurable quantity and makes thermometry physically meaningful.
examples: A mercury thermometer reaches the same temperature as the fluid it measures — the zeroth law guarantees this equivalence | two objects left in contact long enough reach thermal equilibrium
non_examples: Two objects having the same mass or pressure are not necessarily in thermal equilibrium
relates_to: first_law_thermodynamics:PRECEDES | thermodynamic_equilibrium:REQUIRES
confidence: 1.0
note: Called 'zeroth' because it was formalised after the first and second laws but is logically prior — without it temperature has no meaning.
[/TEACH]

concept: first_law_thermodynamics
is_a: AXIOM
definition: The total energy of an isolated system is conserved: ΔU = Q − W, where ΔU is the change in internal energy, Q is heat added to the system, and W is work done by the system. Energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only transformed.
examples: A gas heated in a piston absorbs Q joules, does W joules of work expanding, and its internal energy rises by Q−W | burning fuel converts chemical energy to heat and mechanical work
non_examples: A perpetual motion machine of the first kind — producing work with no energy input — violates this law
requires: internal_energy | heat | thermodynamic_work
relates_to: zeroth_law_thermodynamics:PRECEDES | second_law_thermodynamics:PRECEDES | internal_energy:REQUIRES
confidence: 1.0

concept: second_law_thermodynamics
is_a: AXIOM
definition: In any spontaneous process in an isolated system, the total entropy never decreases. Heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold, never the reverse. No process is possible whose sole result is converting heat completely to work.
examples: Ice melts in warm water — entropy increases | mixing hot and cold gas — entropy increases | heat engines cannot achieve 100% efficiency

confidence: 1.0
note: The most profound asymmetry in physics — it gives time a direction. The second law is why the universe has a past and a future.
[/TEACH]

id: TC_T05
concept: entropy
is_a: CONCEPT
definition: A state function measuring the number of microscopic configurations (microstates) consistent with a system's macroscopic state: S = k_B ln(Ω). Entropy quantifies unavailable energy and the direction of spontaneous change. Higher entropy means more disorder and less available work.
examples: A gas expanding into a vacuum increases entropy — more positions available to molecules | mixing two gases — more microstates than unmixed | melting ice — liquid has far more configurations than crystal
non_examples: Entropy is not simply 'disorder' in everyday sense — a living cell has low entropy but is highly organised internally
requires: second_law_thermodynamics
relates_to: second_law_thermodynamics:REQUIRES | gibbs_free_energy:ENABLES | information_entropy:ANALOGOUS_TO
confidence: 1.0
note: S = k_B ln(Ω) is Boltzmann's equation — engraved on his tombstone. k_B = 1.38e-23 J/K.
[/TEACH]

concept: gibbs_free_energy
is_a: CONCEPT
definition: G = H − TS. The Gibbs free energy determines whether a process at constant temperature and pressure is spontaneous: ΔG < 0 means spontaneous, ΔG > 0 means non-spontaneous, ΔG = 0 means equilibrium. It is the maximum non-expansion work a system can perform.
examples: ATP hydrolysis: ΔG = −30 kJ/mol — spontaneous, drives cellular processes | water boiling at 100°C and 1 atm: ΔG = 0 — liquid and vapour in equilibrium
non_examples: A reaction with ΔH < 0 (exothermic) is not necessarily spontaneous — TΔS might overcome it if T is high enough

id: TC_T08
concept: carnot_cycle
is_a: CONCEPT
definition: An idealised thermodynamic cycle operating between two heat reservoirs at temperatures T_H and T_C, consisting of two isothermal and two adiabatic processes. Its efficiency η = 1 − T_C/T_H is the maximum possible for any heat engine operating between those temperatures.
examples: A Carnot engine between 600 K and 300 K has efficiency 50% — no real engine can exceed this | Carnot efficiency increases as T_C decreases or T_H increases
non_examples: A real steam engine is not a Carnot engine — friction, irreversibility, and finite-time processes all reduce efficiency below the Carnot limit
requires: second_law_thermodynamics | reversible_process
relates_to: second_law_thermodynamics:REQUIRES | heat_engine:ENABLES | reversible_process:REQUIRES
confidence: 1.0
note: The Carnot cycle sets the absolute thermodynamic efficiency ceiling. No engineering improvement can exceed it — only raising T_H or lowering T_C can.
[/TEACH]

concept: heat_engine
is_a: CONCEPT
definition: A device that converts thermal energy (heat) into mechanical work by operating between a hot reservoir and a cold reservoir. Part of the heat input is converted to work; the remainder is rejected to the cold reservoir. Efficiency = W/Q_H = 1 − Q_C/Q_H.
examples: Steam turbine in a power plant: burns fuel to create steam (hot reservoir), turbine extracts work, condenser is cold reservoir | internal combustion engine: explosion is hot reservoir, exhaust is cold
non_examples: An electric motor converting electrical to mechanical energy is not a heat engine — no thermal gradient is involved
requires: first_law_thermodynamics | second_law_thermodynamics

concept: heat_capacity
is_a: CONCEPT
definition: The amount of heat required to raise the temperature of a substance by one degree. C = dQ/dT. At constant pressure: C_p = (∂H/∂T)_P. At constant volume: C_v = (∂U/∂T)_V. For ideal gases, C_p − C_v = nR.
examples: Water has C_p = 4.18 J/g·K — very high, which is why oceans moderate climate | copper has C = 0.39 J/g·K — metals heat up quickly
non_examples: Latent heat is not heat capacity — it's energy for phase transitions at constant temperature

concept: quantum_superposition
is_a: CONCEPT
definition: A quantum system exists in a linear combination of multiple eigenstates simultaneously until measured. examples: Electron spin is in superposition of |up⟩ and |down⟩ until measured | Schrödinger's cat thought experiment | a photon passing through both slits in double-slit experiment
non_examples: A coin toss is NOT superposition — the coin has a definite face down, we just don't know it. Quantum superposition is physically different: the system genuinely lacks a definite value.

non_examples: Observer effect in photography — disturbing the object — is NOT the uncertainty principle. HUP holds even with ideal, non-disturbing measurements.
relates_to: quantum_superposition:REQUIRES | wavefunction:REQUIRES | quantum_measurement:ENABLES

concept: quantum_entanglement
is_a: CONCEPT
definition: Two or more particles in a quantum state that cannot be described independently, even when separated by arbitrary distance. Measuring one particle instantly determines the correlated state of the other. Violates Bell's inequalities, proving no local hidden variable theory can reproduce quantum predictions.
examples: Two electrons in a singlet state — measuring one as spin-up instantly makes the other spin-down regardless of separation | EPR pairs used in quantum cryptography
non_examples: Classical correlation — two gloves in separate boxes, finding one is left-handed tells you the other is right-handed — is not entanglement: the states were predetermined

confidence: 1.0
note: Einstein called it 'spooky action at a distance' and believed it proved QM was incomplete. Bell's theorem in 1964 and subsequent experiments proved Einstein wrong.

concept: quantum_tunneling
is_a: CONCEPT
definition: A quantum particle can penetrate a potential energy barrier that it classically could not overcome. The wavefunction has an exponentially decaying tail inside the barrier — if the barrier is thin enough, significant probability amplitude exists on the other side.
examples: Radioactive alpha decay — alpha particle tunnels through nuclear potential barrier | tunnel diode — electrons tunnel through a thin insulating layer | scanning tunnelling microscope — current tunnels between tip and surface
non_examples: Water flowing under a door is not tunneling — it has a classical path around; tunneling occurs when NO classical path exists
requires: wavefunction | schrodinger_equation
confidence: 1.0
note: Quantum tunneling makes stars shine — proton-proton fusion in the Sun occurs despite classical Coulomb repulsion being orders of magnitude larger than available thermal energy.

concept: pauli_exclusion_principle
is_a: AXIOM
definition: No two identical fermions (particles with half-integer spin) can occupy the same quantum state simultaneously. A consequence of the antisymmetry of fermionic wavefunctions under particle exchange: ψ(1,2) = −ψ(2,1). Bosons (integer spin) are not constrained — they can share states.
examples: Electrons in an atom must have distinct (n, l, m_l, m_s) quantum numbers — this fills shells and gives atoms their chemistry | white dwarf stars are supported against gravity by electron degeneracy pressure (Pauli pressure)
non_examples: Photons (bosons) can all occupy the same state — this enables lasers and Bose-Einstein condensates
requires: quantum_spin
confidence: 1.0

concept: quantum_decoherence
is_a: CONCEPT
definition: The process by which a quantum system loses its coherence (ability to interfere) through entanglement with its environment. The system's reduced density matrix becomes approximately diagonal in the preferred basis — effectively classical. Decoherence does not solve the measurement problem but explains why superpositions are not observed at macroscopic scales.
examples: A large molecule in air decoheres in ~10⁻²³ seconds — too fast to observe quantum behaviour | superconducting qubits must be cooled to milli-Kelvin to maintain coherence | Schrödinger's cat decoheres instantly
non_examples: A single atom in ultra-high vacuum can maintain coherence for seconds — decoherence is environmental, not fundamental

relates_to: quantum_measurement:CAUSES | quantum_entanglement:REQUIRES

note: Bell's theorem is perhaps the most important theorem in the foundations of physics. It converts a philosophical debate into an experimental question — and the experiment answered it definitively.

definition: lim_{x→a} f(x) = L means: for every ε > 0 there exists δ > 0 such that 0 < |x−a| < δ implies |f(x)−L| < ε. The limit describes the value a function approaches, not the value it takes. It is the rigorous foundation of calculus.

concept: typical_set
is_a: CONCEPT
definition: The set of sequences that are 'typical' for a source — their empirical frequencies are close to the true probabilities and their probability is approximately 2^{-nH(X)}. concept: predictive_coding
is_a: CONCEPT
definition: A theory of brain function: higher cortical areas constantly predict the activity of lower areas; only the prediction errors (residuals) are propagated upward. concept: partition_function
is_a: CONCEPT
definition: Z = Σ_s exp(−βE_s) where β = 1/k_BT. All thermodynamic quantities follow from Z: F = −k_BT ln Z (Helmholtz free energy), U = −∂ ln Z/∂β (internal energy), S = k_B(ln Z + βU) (entropy). The partition function encodes the entire thermodynamic content of a statistical mechanical model.
